newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia sees volatile world coffee prices.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia sees volatile world coffee prices.

text.p: International coffee prices are expected to be volatile over the next two months because of a frost scare in top exporter Brazil but rates could dip if the weather holds, a spokesman for Indonesian exporters said on Wednesday.

Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters, said a meeting of major coffee producers was scheduled in London in September to discuss their export quotas "because the (frost) picture will be clear by then".
"If prices are going down (now), it's because the cold winds (in Brazil) are blowing into the sea," he told Reuters on the sidelines of a seminar on coffee in Jakarta.

"This is the season of the frost scare (in Brazil). Fears of a frost will be at the peak in early August. But nobody can say whether there will be a frost or not," he said. "The market will be manipulated in that duration."
New York coffee futures fell sharply on Tuesday as weather forecasts of warmer temperatures in Brazil and a bearish tehnical outlook sparked panicky speculative selling.
The spot July arabica coffee contract plunged 35.35 cents a lb on the day to a one-month low of 217.95 cents. Second-month September fell 26.85 cents to 196.75.

Earlier in the day, London's July robusta coffee contract made an about-face to close $65 lower at $1,825 a tonne after gaining $70 by midsession. September also gave up the day's advance to finish $75 down at $1,850.
Independent weather forecaster Weather Services Corporation said on Wednesday no damaging cold was expected through early next week in Brazil's coffee regions.
Soedargo said that if Brazil survived the frost scare, prices of coffee would fall. "After the frost scare...if there is no frost, prices will come down," he said.
"If conditions are normal, if there is no shortage or other factors, prices should be around $1,500," he said.
He also said the 14-member Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) will meet in September to discuss its export programme.
"I don't know what decision will be taken during the meeting, but it will have to consider the situation in Brazil. It's crucial," he said.

The ACPC decided last month to extend its export restrictions by 12 months to July 1, setting a ceiling of 52.75 million bags. The grouping said individual quotas of members would be set at a meeting in September.
"When the ACPC meets in September, the picture will be clear by then," he said, referring to the frost scare in Brazil. "By then we should know where the market will head," he said.
Indonesia, Asia's sole ACPC member and the world's top robusta producer, was given an export quota of six million bags during the 1996/97 (July-June) ACPC export programme.

Industry sources said Indonesian exporters would be happy if their quota was maintained in the next programme as they expected a production shortfall this year due to bad weather and there would be no need to hold back sales.
